title: In a hurry
hookLine: seminary students hurrying to talk about the Good Samaritan often passed a person in need (Darley and Batson)

cards: "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves."

That's how Jesus begins the parable of the Good Samaritan in the Gospel of Luke, as the King James Version has it, the story this path met back on day seventy-seven. Robbed, beaten, left half dead by the road.
A priest comes by and passes on the other side. A Levite does the same. Then a Samaritan, a traveler from Samaria, stops, binds his wounds, and pays for his care.
Some readers ask why the first two walked past. A pair of psychologists decided to find out what might make anyone walk past.

teach.h: A TALK ON THE GOOD SAMARITAN.
teach.b: First, the setup. John Darley and Daniel Batson recruited students at a theological seminary and asked each to prepare a short talk: some on jobs for ministers, some on the parable of the Good Samaritan itself.
Then each was sent across campus to give it in another building. Second, the clock.
Before they left, some were told they were late and had to hurry. Others were told they had a few minutes, or plenty of time.

teach.h: A MAN SLUMPED IN A DOORWAY.
teach.b: Third, the man in the doorway. On the way, each student passed a man slumped in an alley, head down, coughing and groaning. He was part of the study.
The students in a hurry stopped far less often than the ones with time. And here's the sting: the topic of the talk made little difference.
Students on their way to speak about the Good Samaritan were not much more likely to help.
The researchers reported that on some occasions, a student hurrying to talk about the parable literally stepped over the man to get there.
The parable never says why the priest and the Levite passed by, and the study doesn't claim to know either. But it raises a plain possibility: not hard hearts, just full calendars.
A week about compassion as something real and trainable ends with a very ordinary obstacle. Not cruelty. Hurry.

how: Christians read the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) as a teaching about who counts as a neighbor; some people build slack into their day on purpose, leaving early so there's room to notice and help.

games.q: you're a seminary student, late for your talk on the Good Samaritan. a man is slumped in a doorway, groaning. what did hurried students mostly do?
o: stop and help, because of the talk's topic.
pass by on the way to the talk.
go back and fetch someone else.
games.why: students in a hurry stopped far less often, even those about to speak on the parable itself.

practice: Look at the rest of today and find one trip, meeting or pickup where you usually arrive just in time, or a little late, and picture leaving five minutes earlier for it.
See those spare minutes on the way, room to notice a face, a dropped bag, a person who looks lost, then rest in the breath, in no hurry at all.

wordCard.voice: In a hurry. In one study, seminary students rushing to talk about the Good Samaritan often passed a man in need; hurry mattered more than the topic. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: not in a hurry. Five spare minutes leave room to look up. That's the week.
